Q: How can I translate the recover password email in October CMS A:

Translating email templates in October CMS (specifically for the RainLab.User plugin) requires a specific workflow. Since the email content is usually stored in the database or as a static file, standard Twig translation filters like |_ often don't work as expected if the locale isn't explicitly set during the mail-sending process.

Here are the two best ways to achieve this:

Using Multi-language Email Templates

October CMS supports localized mail templates natively. You don't need to create files like recover_password-de.htm. Instead, you use the built-in localization feature in the backend.

  1. Navigate to Settings > Mail > Mail Templates.

  2. Find the rainlab.user::mail.restore (or user:recover_password) template.

  3. If you have the RainLab.Translate plugin installed, you should see a locale switcher (e.g., EN, DE, FR) within the mail template editor.

  4. Switch to the desired language and enter the translated subject and body content.

Note: For this to work automatically, the user's locale must be stored in their profile. October CMS will try to use the $user->locale attribute to decide which version to send.

Q: implicit declaration of function usleep A:

That list is the pre-conditions for having usleep defined. It's basically a C-like expression involving #define variables which has to be true before including the header file.

The header file itself will only define usleep inside what is usually a massive nest of #ifdef statements and the developers have taken the time to tell you what you need to do so that you don't have to spend hours trying to figure it out yourself :-)

Assuming you're using a glibc 2.12 or better, it means you either have to:

  • define _BSD_SOURCE; or
  • define a more complicated combination of three other things, which I won't bother to decode.

Probably the easiest fix is to simply compile with gcc -D _BSD_SOURCE or put:

#define _BSD_SOURCE

in the code before you include the header file that gives you usleep.

You'll probably want to define these before any includes in case there are dependencies between the various header files.

Q: Selenium ChromeDriver randomly crashes with 'session deleted because of page crash' error even in headless mode A:

Chrome v120 & ChromeDriver v120 is old and outdated. Accordingly the failure reasons can be numerous. Additionally you haven't mentioned the Selenium version you are using.

Solution

Ensure the following:

  • Chrome Browser is updated to current chrome=143.0
  • Selenium is upgraded to current released Version 4.39.0 and let the in-built Selenium Manager download the matching ChromeDriver for the program execution.

Your minimal code block can be:

from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options

options = Options()
options.add_argument("--headless")
options.add_argument("--screen-info={0,0 1920x1080}")

driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
try:
    driver.get("https://example.com")
    print(driver.title)
finally:
    driver.quit()

tl; dr

Note:

  • With Chrome in headless mode --window-size=1920,1080 no longer works and you need to use --screen-info={0,0 1920x1080}
  • Avoid using the options --no-sandbox, --disable-dev-shm-usage, --disable-gpu, etc unless they are absolutely necessary.

Q: Is std::system thread safe? If not, in which way? A:

As specified in its warning description, clang-tidy either considers POSIX, glibc or "any libc" when determining the thread-safety, depending on the used FunctionSet option.

POSIX 2008 states that

The system() function need not be thread-safe

Therefore the warning is appropriate for the posix function set.

As stated in Is it safe to call system(3) from multi-threaded process?, Solaris 10 has a non-thread-safe system() function. Therefore the warning is also appropriate for the any function set.

glibc has a thread-safe system() implementation, therefore the glibc function set should not issue a warning.

We can also look at other standards. C11 states in section 7.1.4, paragraph 5:

Unless explicitly stated otherwise in the detailed descriptions that follow, library functions shall prevent data races as follows: A library function shall not directly or indirectly access objects accessible by threads other than the current thread unless the objects are accessed directly or indirectly via the function’s arguments. A library function shall not directly or indirectly modify objects accessible by threads other than the current thread unless the objects are accessed directly or indirectly via the function’s non-const arguments) Implementations may share their own internal objects between threads if the objects are not visible to users and are protected against data races

system() is not explicitly exempt from this, therefore any conforming C11 implementation has to have a thread-safe system() function.

C++11 and upwards contains similar language:

A C++ standard library function shall not directly or indirectly modify objects ([intro.multithread]) accessible by threads other than the current thread unless the objects are accessed directly or indirectly via the function's non-const arguments, including this.

[Note 1: This means, for example, that implementations can't use an object with static storage duration for internal purposes without synchronization because doing so can cause a data race even in programs that do not explicitly share objects between threads.
— end note]

system() is included in the C++ standard library, therefore the rule should apply.
